messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Train Conductor
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 43

He is 29, a single Middle Eastern man who has worked as a train conductor for several years, and he still organizes his life by timetables, routes, and the small rituals that make a long shift feel predictable. Before the event, he likes the comfort of repetition: checking doors, calling out stations, watching passengers move in waves at the same familiar platforms. He takes pride in being calm under pressure. Coworkers know him as dependable, the one who notices when something is off.

The day that stays with him begins like any other. It is early evening, and the platform is crowded with commuters. He remembers the smell of wet concrete from a recent rain, the metallic screech as the train pulls in, and the blur of umbrellas closing as people press forward. As he steps out to monitor boarding, he notices shouting near the edge of the platform. At first it registers as ordinary commuter frustration, the kind of sharp exchange he sees all the time. Then he sees one man stumble backward. The scene changes too quickly for him to make sense of it. The man falls onto the tracks just as the train is entering the station.

He remembers the impact in fragments rather than as a continuous sequence. The driver slams the brakes. People scream. Someone grabs his arm, but he pulls away and runs toward the front cars because training takes over before thought does. He hears himself shouting for emergency services, hears his own voice sounding strange and far away. He sees the body beneath the train and, even now, cannot speak about that moment directly without his face going blank. What returns to him most often is not the image itself but one detail: a single shoe lying upright near the yellow line, untouched in the chaos.

In the hours afterward he functions automatically. He gives statements, answers questions, repeats the timeline to transit police and supervisors. Everyone tells him he did what he was supposed to do. He nods. That night, back in his apartment, he cannot take off his uniform for a long time. When he finally lies down, every time he closes his eyes he sees the platform again, then the shoe, then the sudden movement of the crowd pulling back. He does not really sleep. By morning he feels as if the event is still happening.

He returns to work sooner than his family thinks he should. Part of him believes routine will fix it. Instead, the station feels altered, as if danger now lives inside places that used to be ordinary. He starts scanning every platform edge, every impatient passenger, every person standing too close to the tracks. If someone sways even slightly, his chest tightens. The sound of brakes makes his whole body jolt. He finds himself barking at passengers to stand back with more force than he intends, then feeling ashamed when they stare at him.

At home, he becomes difficult to reach. His younger sister calls him and he lets it ring. Friends invite him out after shift, but restaurants near stations make him uneasy, and crowded places feel impossible. He tells people he is tired, which is true, but not in the simple way they mean. Sleep comes in short stretches broken by the same nightmare: he is on the platform but cannot move, cannot shout, cannot stop what he knows is about to happen. He wakes with his heart pounding, sometimes already halfway out of bed.

He begins avoiding reminders in ways that surprise him. He takes longer routes through stations so he does not have to pass the exact platform. During breaks, he sits in maintenance rooms instead of the staff lounge because casual conversation feels unbearable. News clips about transit accidents make him nauseated, but he cannot stop searching for them online late at night, as if he might find some missing explanation that will settle his mind. He tells himself he should have seen more, moved faster, done something different, even though another part of him knows that thought makes no sense.

Over time, he notices changes in himself that feel larger than fear. He is more irritable, especially with passengers who are intoxicated or distracted by their phones near the tracks. He startles when someone approaches him from behind. He rarely feels fully off duty. On days he is not working, he still hears phantom station announcements in his apartment and catches himself looking out the window when he hears the distant rumble of trains. His world has narrowed to work, home, and the effort of staying composed.

When he speaks about the event now, several sessions in, he does so carefully, circling it before getting close. He says the hardest part is that everyone else seems to have placed it in the past. For him it remains immediate, stored not as a memory but as a live possibility. Each platform edge still carries the feeling that something terrible is about to happen again, and his body responds as though it is his job, every moment, to prevent the next disaster.
